sections.authorBiography: William Shakespeare was baptized in Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564, the son of John Shakespeare, a glover and town official, and Mary Arden. He probably attended Stratford's grammar school, married Anne Hathaway in 1582, and had three children: Susanna and the twins Hamnet and Judith (Hamnet died aged eleven in 1596). By the early 1590s he was an actor and playwright in London; from 1594 he was a sharer in the Lord Chamberlain's Men, who built the Globe theatre in 1599 and became the King's Men when James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603. He wrote or co-wrote about 38 plays and the Sonnets, and died in Stratford on 23 April 1616. Seven years later his fellow actors John Heminges and Henry Condell published 36 of his plays in the First Folio (1623).
sections.historicalContext: Hamlet was probably written between about 1599 and 1601, after Julius Caesar, for the Lord Chamberlain's Men at the Globe; Richard Burbage played the prince. Its story goes back to the Danish chronicle of Saxo Grammaticus (the tale of Amleth, written around 1200), retold in French by François de Belleforest (1570). An earlier English Hamlet play, now lost and often called the "Ur-Hamlet," was on stage by 1589, when Thomas Nashe joked about it. Revenge tragedy was a popular genre, following Thomas Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy (c. 1587). The play draws on live questions of its time: Protestant doubts about purgatory and ghosts (Hamlet studies at Wittenberg, Luther's university), the duty and danger of revenge, and succession, since Elizabeth I was old and had no heir.

publicationAndReception.publication: Hamlet survives in three early texts: a short First Quarto (1603), a long Second Quarto (1604–05) and the First Folio (1623), which differ in many lines and in whole passages. Modern editions, including the reading text here, combine them. It is Shakespeare's longest play.
publicationAndReception.then: It was popular at once: the Cambridge scholar Gabriel Harvey wrote in the margin of a book that it pleased "the wiser sort," and the First Quarto's title page says it had been acted in London and at Cambridge and Oxford. After 1660 it remained one of the most performed tragedies; the Romantic writers Goethe and Coleridge made Hamlet's divided mind the centre of interpretation.
publicationAndReception.now: Hamlet is perhaps the most performed and written-about play in the world. Readings have been psychological (Freud and Ernest Jones's Oedipal theory), political, feminist (Ophelia's madness and silencing) and existential. Films include Laurence Olivier's (1948), Grigori Kozintsev's (1964) and Kenneth Branagh's (1996); Disney's The Lion King (1994) borrows its plot. Lines such as "To be, or not to be" and "Something is rotten in the state of Denmark" are part of everyday English.

sections.overview: Prince Hamlet returns to Denmark for his father's funeral and finds his uncle Claudius on the throne, married to his mother Gertrude. Guards on the castle walls have seen a ghost that looks like the dead king. What the ghost tells Hamlet, and what Hamlet does and fails to do about it, is the play.

sections.whyItMatters: Hamlet is the great play about thinking: about how hard it is to know the truth, to act rightly when you are unsure, and to live with grief, anger and doubt. Its questions about revenge, mental health, family loyalty and political corruption remain urgent, and its language is the most quoted in English.

spoilerOverview.text: The Ghost says Claudius murdered him and demands revenge. Hamlet feigns madness, rejects Ophelia, and stages a play (The Mousetrap) that confirms Claudius's guilt. He spares Claudius at prayer, then kills Polonius, hidden behind a curtain, by mistake. Claudius sends Hamlet to England to be executed; Hamlet escapes, sending Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to their deaths. Ophelia goes mad and drowns. Laertes returns for revenge, and Claudius plots a rigged fencing match with a poisoned blade and poisoned wine. Gertrude drinks the poison; Laertes and Hamlet are both wounded with the poisoned blade; Hamlet kills Claudius and dies in Horatio's arms. Fortinbras of Norway takes the throne.

segments.phase: I do: the book in one passage
segments.activity: Model a close reading of one passage using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Something is rotten in the state of Denmark” slowly and put it in my own words: After the Ghost appears and beckons Hamlet away, the guard Marcellus says that something is rotten in the state of Denmark. Next, craft. I notice the image of decay applied to a whole country, as if the kingdom were a body going bad. The strongest word is “rotten”: it suggests corruption spreading from inside, which fits a murder hidden at the top of the state. Then, effect. What does Marcellus's line suggest about Denmark at the start of the play? My answer: Marcellus senses that the Ghost means a moral sickness in Denmark's rulers; the image of rot runs through the play, as Claudius's secret crime poisons the court, the family and Hamlet's mind.

segments.activity: Exit ticket on the author and context (answer given).
segments.script: Shakespeare wrote Hamlet around 1600, near the end of Queen Elizabeth I's reign, when no one knew who would succeed her, and revenge tragedies were popular on the London stage. How might that context shape a play about a disputed throne and revenge? Answer: Accept answers such as: worry about succession made a stolen crown feel urgent; audiences knew the revenge-play formula and Shakespeare questions it; the play reflects anxiety about legitimate rule.

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this scene, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Hamlet.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Hamlet: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

answerKey.answer: Another prince who has lost a father.
As foils to compare responses to loss and revenge.
To keep secret what they saw and his plan.
Laertes's answer when asked what he would do to Hamlet.
Hamlet holds the skull of the jester he loved as a child.
He is "son to the late, and nephew to the present king," and Gertrude is "queen of Denmark, and mother to Hamlet," so loyalty to his father and to the court are already in conflict.
The Ghost demands "Revenge his foul and most unnatural murder," and Hamlet ends with "The time is out of joint: O cursed spite, / That ever I was born to set it right!"
He tells Reynaldo to "By indirections find directions out," and after Ophelia's report decides "This is the very ecstasy of love."
Claudius admits "my offence is rank," Hamlet hesitates ("Now might I do it pat, now he is praying"), but Claudius admits "My words fly up, my thoughts remain below."
He calls him a sponge "that soaks up the king's countenance" and riddles "The body is with the king, but the king is not with the body."
He cries "To hell, allegiance!" while Claudius notes "sorrows come... in battalions" and Ophelia gives "rosemary, that's for remembrance."
He tells Horatio "There's a divinity that shapes our ends," says "the readiness is all," kills Claudius only after the poison is revealed, and dies with "The rest is silence."

criticalVoices.quote: But what Hamlet wanted was not a private revenge, to be followed by his own imprisonment or execution; it was public justice.
criticalVoices.speaker: A. C. Bradley, Oxford Professor of Poetry
criticalVoices.source: Shakespearean Tragedy (1904), Lecture III, Lecture III, section on the "external difficulties" theory
criticalVoices.useNote: Careful attribution: Bradley is summarizing a view he goes on to reject (Hamlet's obstacles were external). Students who use it must say so, then decide: does V.ii give us private revenge or public justice?
